A man in his 80s was brought to the emergency department after a cardiac arrest. According to paramedics, the patient was last seen healthy by his family 4 hours earlier, then was found unresponsive and pulseless in the bathroom. He underwent cardiopulmonary resuscitation, receiving 4 doses of epinephrine intravenously and endotracheal tube intubation with return of spontaneous circulation after approximately 10 minutes. Family later revealed he had chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and had been complaining of shortness of breath for 2 days prior to presentation. A healthy 27-year-old Hispanic man presented with a 3-month history of daily fevers with chills, night sweats, generalized weakness, a 25-pound weight loss, poor appetite, and a sore throat. No history of recent infections, trauma, surgery, or travel. Review of systems was negative for shortness of breath, cough, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and changes in bowel or urinary habits.

Temperature: 37.8 °C, heart rate: 118 beats/minute with regular rhythm, blood pressure: 103/67 mm Hg, respiratory rate: 18 cycles/min. Cardiovascular and pulmonary examination were unremarkable. Right knee effusion present with no other inflamed joints. Nonpruritic, palpable, brown macular rash on the chest and back noted.

Laboratory Tests:
- Leukocyte count: 28.7 × 10⁹/L (normal: 3.5–10.5)
- Hemoglobin: 87 g/L (normal: 135–175)
- Platelet count: 750 × 10⁹/L (normal: 150–450)
- Serum electrolyte and renal function: Normal
- Aspartate aminotransferase: 2.02 µkat/L (normal: 0.17–0.67)
- Alanine aminotransferase: 1.79 µkat/L (normal: ≤0.91)
- Alkaline phosphatase: 6.97 µkat/L (normal: 0.67–2.5)
- Lactate dehydrogenase: 7.52 µkat/L (normal: 1.98–3.92)
- Ferritin: 29,161 µg/L (normal: 22–275)

Synovial Fluid Analysis:
- Leukocyte count: 10.1 × 10⁹/L with 97% neutrophils
- Cultures: Negative

Imaging:
- CT scan: Diffuse hepatomegaly

Biopsy Results:

- Pericardial tissue: Marked acute inflammation with prominent neutrophilic infiltrates and numerous histiocytes

A 61-year-old woman with cirrhosis secondary to alcohol use disorder in remission. Past medical history included esophageal varices, rectal varices, ascites, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, and recurrent pleural effusion. Risk factors included a remote history of intranasal cocaine use and multiple tattoos. No history of blood transfusions before 1990, intravenous drug use, or high-risk sexual behavior. Three years after initial evaluation, she developed clinical decompensation requiring multiple paracenteses, thoracenteses, and blood transfusions for gastrointestinal bleeding. Three months into this period of decline, she had a dental extraction.

Patient presented with hepatic encephalopathy, acute kidney injury, and recurrent pleural effusion. Mental status showed acute decline. Progressive deterioration led to increased encephalopathy with concurrent hypotension requiring critical care unit transfer.

Nine hours following the operation, the patient experienced recurrent right abdomen pain progressing to involve the entire abdomen, with persistent nausea and perceived increase in body temperature.

Initial examination showed tenderness in the right abdomen, without rebound tenderness and muscular tension, with normal bowel sounds. Later examination revealed diffuse tenderness with rebound tenderness, primarily in the right abdomen. Dullness to percussion was observed, while pain during percussion in the liver area was absent. A 65-year-old woman presented with blurry vision in her right eye for several months. Ocular history included 3 recurrent episodes of bilateral iritis occurring during 5 months, amblyopia in the left eye, and bilateral posterior chamber intraocular lens. Right eye showed trace conjunctival injection without definite ciliary flush, 2+ fine keratic precipitates, and 1+ cells in the anterior chamber. Left eye had a few keratic precipitates. Dilated fundus examination revealed cystoid macular edema with a yellow spot in the fovea in the right eye and an epiretinal membrane in the left eye. Over the preceding 3 months, he had left buttock and greater trochanteric pain, initially attributed to overuse. He denied fevers or systemic symptoms. On examination, range of motion of the left hip was full and painless; there was focal tenderness over the posterior buttock and greater trochanter but no palpable mass. A diagnosis of greater trochanteric bursitis was made, and an intra‐bursal corticosteroid injection was administered, resulting in partial symptom relief.

Six weeks later, he returned with persistent buttock pain and intermittent electric shock–like sensations radiating down the left leg. Physical examination now revealed decreased and painful range of motion of the left hip with continued tenderness over the greater trochanter. A lumbar spine radiograph was normal. A 15-year-old girl presented with multiple swellings of five months’ duration. She noted progressive enlargement of bilateral neck masses and one each on her back and anterior abdominal wall, without pain. There was no significant past medical, personal, or family history.

Complete blood count, metabolic panel, and skeletal survey were all normal. With a clinical impression of lymphoreticular malignancy or metastatic disease, fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) was performed on the most prominent swellings (two cervical, one paraspinal, one abdominal).

The spindle cells had bipolar cytoplasmic extensions and round-to-oval nuclei with fine granular chromatin; nucleoli were inconspicuous. clinical_record:
A 14-year-old Caucasian girl was transferred from a community emergency department after treatment for presumed anaphylaxis following ingestion of a hypoallergenic nutritional supplement. Immediately after ingestion she reported wheezing, cough, and swelling of the lips, face, and tongue and self-administered epinephrine (0.3 mg) at home. Her history included suspected food allergies (wheat, oats, tree nuts, chocolate, eggs, cow’s milk, and rice) without documented reactions; intermittent asthma; complex regional pain syndrome; delayed gastric emptying; and major depressive disorder treated with fluoxetine, increased to 60 mg daily 5 months earlier. Skin prick tests and serum-specific IgE to foods of concern were negative except for sensitization to several tree nuts without a supportive history of reaction with ingestion. Testing for hereditary angioedema and baseline serum tryptase were normal. She had lost 40 lb over the past year through dietary restriction and exercise and was homeschooled due to fears of allergic reactions.

In the ED she had stridor, biphasic wheezing, and poor air movement without visible oropharyngeal swelling. She was afebrile, blood pressure 94/48 mmHg, heart rate 100 bpm, respiratory rate 30/min, and SpO₂ 100% on room air. She received IV fluids, two doses of subcutaneous epinephrine, inhaled bronchodilators, racemic epinephrine, and antihistamines, and was admitted to the PICU. Her presumed angioedema resolved with treatment.

Over the next several weeks in an eating-disorder program, she had seven similar episodes requiring ED evaluation and PICU admission. Each episode featured subjective perioral swelling, hypotension within her baseline range, and stridor that resolved without objective edema. Direct laryngoscopy during one episode showed no airway edema or paradoxical vocal cord motion. Serial serum tryptase levels during acute events remained normal, a bone marrow biopsy was equivocal, and further workup—including complement levels, mast cell mediators, urine prostaglandins, complete blood count, and metabolic panel—was unremarkable. She was managed with daily antihistamines, ranitidine, cromolyn, and a tapering course of prednisone; rescue therapy included cetirizine and lorazepam. She continued to experience suicidal ideation and auditory hallucinations and was started on aripiprazole.

A 32-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks 3 days of gestation presented with acute left lower abdominal pain and vomiting. She denied vaginal bleeding, urinary symptoms, constipation, or changes in bowel habits. Her observations were stable, and she appeared clinically well. On examination, there was slight tenderness in the left abdomen without guarding; the uterus was soft and relaxed. Foetal movements and monitoring were normal.

Her antenatal course had been uneventful except for a 70 × 60 × 60 mm left ovarian cyst first noted at 5 weeks and thought to be endometriotic. Follow-up scans at 32 weeks showed the cyst measured 63 × 33 × 69 mm with internal echoes and an avascular solid component. Tumour markers (CEA, CA-19-9, CA-125) were within normal limits, and an MDT review deemed the cyst benign and recommended surveillance.

On admission, Hb was 121 g/L, WCC 10.0 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 9.1 × 10^9/L, platelets 270 × 10^9/L, and CRP 30 mg/L. Over three days, CRP rose to 209 mg/L while WCC remained stable. Repeated transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasounds by an experienced sonographer showed the left adnexal cyst unchanged in size and appearance with no whirlpool sign, stromal oedema, absent Doppler flow, or free pelvic fluid. MRI was considered but not performed due to the rapid clinical change.

At 37 weeks 1 day, her pain worsened with vomiting, and abdominal exam revealed generalized tenderness with guarding in the left iliac fossa. Given the acute abdomen, rising inflammatory markers, and concern for ovarian torsion, the decision was made to proceed with a caesarean section followed by surgical management of the adnexa.

A 35-year-old man from rural north India presented with a one-month history of a progressively enlarging, central abdominal lump. Three weeks after the lump appeared, he developed intermittent high-grade fever and dull, aching abdominal pain. He had no significant past medical history. On examination, there was a moderately tender mass in the umbilical region. There was non-tender thickening of the right spermatic cord without scrotal or testicular abnormalities; inguinal nodes were barely palpable, and there was no lower-extremity edema. Complete blood counts and blood chemistry were within normal limits, and blood cultures were sterile. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a large, well-defined, unilocular cyst measuring 20 × 14 × 23 cm located behind the right colon and terminal ileum, without features suggestive of an abscess; the remainder of the abdominal organs appeared normal. Contrast-enhanced CT scan confirmed these findings but did not clarify the origin or etiology of the cyst. Because of diagnostic uncertainty and ongoing symptoms, the abdomen was explored surgically, revealing a large retroperitoneal cyst posterior to the right colon, mesocolon, and terminal ileum that stretched adjacent structures; a well-defined avascular plane allowed complete excision of the cyst, and a conglomeration of grossly dilated lymphatics near its upper pole was also removed.

A 55-year-old right-handed man with no significant medical history presented with two days of worsening “heaviness” in his right arm. He denied gait difficulty, pain, sensory changes, or cranial symptoms. He had an upper respiratory illness three weeks earlier and denied diarrhea or recent vaccinations. On arrival, blood pressure was 220/139 mm Hg; he was afebrile and alert. Examination showed uniform weakness of the right upper extremity (motor strength 3/5) with 1+ reflexes; left upper extremity and bilateral lower extremities had strength 5/5 with 2+ reflexes. Sensation was intact, cranial nerves were normal, and he walked unassisted. Urine toxicology, head CT, brain MRI with diffusion‐weighted imaging, and cervical‐spine imaging were all unremarkable. He was admitted for observation. On hospital day 2, lumbar puncture showed 1 white blood cell, no red blood cells, and protein 33 mg/dL. Serum assay for botulinum toxin was negative. On hospital day 3, right arm strength declined to 2/5, and new left arm weakness (4/5) appeared; repeat MRI remained normal. On hospital day 4, he was unable to walk unassisted, had complete flaccid paralysis of the right arm, left arm strength 3/5, and areflexia throughout all extremities.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

The clinical picture (pure motor, ascending flaccid paralysis, areflexia, normal CSF protein, post-URI, no sensory loss) strongly favors AMAN over AIDP, so the unqualified parent label is insufficient.
Acute motor axonal neuropathy is an axonal motor variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome; the generic label omits the benchmark subtype.

A 61-year-old man with a 20-year history of recurrent episodes of abdominal pain, bloating, and obstipation, alternating with intermittent diarrhea, and a 30-lb weight loss presented for evaluation. His history included heavy alcohol use (12–24 beers daily for 20 years) and an uncomplicated cholecystectomy 10 years earlier, after which symptoms began eight days postoperatively. Over the next decade, colonoscopy and esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed no abnormalities, “including any evidence of celiac disease.” A trial of conservative management failed, and exploratory laparotomy “showed no mechanical cause of the obstructions.” Alcohol use stopped 2 years ago because of worsening symptoms. Fifteen months after the first surgery, a CT scan showed small-bowel dilation (approximately 23 mm in diameter) consistent with obstruction and a concurrent megacolon dilated up to 15 cm. Laboratory studies revealed low levels of fat-soluble vitamins: vitamin A 22 µg/dL (reference, 32.5–78.0), vitamin D 7 ng/mL (20–50), vitamin E 4.3 mg/L (5.5–17), and vitamin K 2.65 ng/mL (0.23–3.2). A gluten-free diet trialed for 3 months produced no improvement.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

However, the record does not provide definitive evidence to specify visceral myopathy over other potential causes of pseudo-obstruction, such as visceral neuropathy. It is a more specific cause than the requested diagnosis, but the requested diagnosis is a syndrome, not a specific etiology.

An 82-year-old man presented with painless right testicular swelling of several weeks’ duration without systemic symptoms. His history included glaucoma, prostatic adenomectomy, and hernioplasty; medications were dorzolamide, lansoprazole, and dutasteride. Testicular ultrasound showed enlargement and inhomogeneity of the right testis and epididymis with ipsilateral hydrocele. After 10 days of amoxicillin–clavulanate for presumed orchiepididymitis, swelling persisted. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT confirmed testicular pathology and revealed new bilateral macronodular adrenal enlargement measuring 15×12 mm on the right and 27×18 mm on the left, with homogeneous attenuation; these nodules were absent on a CT scan 3 years earlier. An 18 FDG PET/CT showed intense uptake (SUVmax 25.5) in the right testis but no uptake in the adrenal glands. Laboratory evaluation revealed normal electrolytes, blood count, iron studies, protein electrophoresis, glucose, renal and liver function, thyroid profile, LDH, and β2-microglobulin. Serologies were negative for active HCV and EBV (positive for past EBV). Clinically, he had no asthenia, headaches, abdominal pain, striae, or “buffalo hump,” and his blood pressure was 130/80 mmHg without hypertensive peaks on 24-hour monitoring.

A 19-year-old man with hepatitis C and intravenous heroin use was transferred for evaluation of altered mental status. He was found minimally responsive and arrived febrile and intermittently responsive (Glasgow Coma Scale 10), requiring intubation for airway protection. On examination, he had left upper- and lower-limb weakness (strength 2/5 and 3/5) without meningeal signs. Vital signs were stable. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (white blood cell count rising from 10.0 to 14.6 × 10^3/µL). Urine toxicology was positive for benzodiazepines and opiates. 

Noncontrast head CT demonstrated a hypodense area in the right basal ganglia with mass effect but no hemorrhage. Brain MRI revealed T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the right basal ganglia and internal capsule with mild surrounding edema, scattered small foci of restricted diffusion, and subtle punctate blooming on susceptibility-weighted images; there was no enhancement after gadolinium. Transthoracic echocardiography showed no valvular vegetations.

Lumbar puncture yielded an opening pressure of 23 cm H₂O and slightly hazy cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with 538 WBCs/mm³ (57% polymorphonuclear leukocytes), protein 81 mg/dL, and glucose 57 mg/dL (serum 121 mg/dL); Gram stain was negative. Initial CSF studies were negative for acid-fast bacilli, herpes simplex virus PCR, and fungi. Empirical IV ceftriaxone, vancomycin, and acyclovir were begun; his leukocytosis improved but fever persisted. 

On hospital day 5 he became more obtunded. Repeat lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 30 cm H₂O, 1762 WBCs/mm³ (60% polymorphonuclear leukocytes), protein 123 mg/dL, glucose 30 mg/dL (serum 105 mg/dL), and no red cells. Rickettsial studies, multiple viral cultures including John Cunningham virus PCR, quantiferon gold, and protozoal investigations were also negative. Repeat MRI demonstrated progression with new involvement of the left basal ganglia, increased diffusion restriction, development of necrosis, and new peripheral contrast enhancement. 

Because the etiology remained unclear and the patient was deteriorating, a brain biopsy was planned.

clinical_record:
An 18-year-old African male with no prior medical history presented first with a 2-day history of tonsillitis and a new macular rash on his chest that extended to his arms. Three days later he developed abdominal cramping and multiple episodes of non-bloody, watery diarrhea without nausea or vomiting, along with fevers and joint pains in his wrists, elbows, and knees. Initial outpatient care included oral chlorhexidine, lozenges, and symptomatic treatment.

He was then seen at a local health facility with high fever, tachycardia, and within 24 hours became confused with rising serum creatinine (from 200 to 400 μmol/L). He received ceftriaxone, paracetamol, loperamide, and one dose of IV methylprednisolone, but continued to deteriorate and was transferred to our hospital.

On arrival he was febrile (40°C), hypotensive (70/40 mmHg), tachycardic (130 bpm), tachypneic (50 breaths/min), and hypoxemic (SaO2 86% on room air). GCS was 14/15. Lung exam revealed bilaterally coarse crepitations; cardiovascular exam an audible S3 gallop; abdomen distended and tense with hypoactive bowel sounds; musculoskeletal exam was normal. He received fluid resuscitation, central line placement, and norepinephrine at 0.4 μg/kg/min.

Laboratory data showed: WBC 27.1×10^9/L; Hb 10.9 g/dL; platelets 281×10^9/L; procalcitonin 71.6 ng/mL; CRP 287 mg/L; creatinine 494 μmol/L; urea 26.7 mmol/L; Na 128 mmol/L; K 4.87 mmol/L; HCO3– 15.5 mmol/L; blood gas pH 7.33, PCO2 23 mmHg, PO2 122 mmHg, HCO3– 19.8 mmol/L. Liver tests showed AST 1461 U/L and ALT 812 U/L; hepatitis A, B, C, and HIV screens were negative. Urinalysis had 3+ protein and 4+ blood without RBCs; urine albumin:creatinine ratio was 52.3 mg/mmol. Cardiac markers were elevated (troponin 17 137 ng/mL; CK > 7800 U/L).

A negative ASOT made rheumatic fever unlikely. Chest X-ray showed pulmonary edema and cardiomegaly; echocardiogram revealed dilated cardiomyopathy with EF 30–35% and normal valves. Abdominal CT demonstrated a distended bowel with splenic and renal infarcts. HRCT confirmed cardiomegaly with bi-basal atelectasis. Initial differentials included bacterial septic shock, vasculitis (antiphospholipid syndrome or medium-sized vessel vasculitis), and multisystem inflammatory syndrome.

He required intubation and increasing norepinephrine (0.7 μg/kg/min), meropenem, vancomycin, urgent dialysis, and cooling measures. An autoimmune panel showed low C3 (0.51 g/L) and C4 (0.04 g/L), and he received a low-dose steroid pulse (250 mg IV daily). Autoantibodies returned with a positive beta2-glycoprotein IgA antiphospholipid antibody and negative ANA, anti–dsDNA, ENA, pANCA, and cANCA. SARS-CoV-2 PCR from tracheal aspirate and nasal swab was negative.

A 29-year-old Caucasian man with a history of hepatitis C, posttraumatic stress disorder, polysubstance abuse, and tobacco use was brought to the emergency department after being found agitated and erratically wandering the streets and then unresponsive with multiple skin abrasions. He reported ingestion and insufflation of “bath salts,” a history later confirmed by his family. He denied other medications or supplements and had no known drug allergies.

On examination, temperature was 107°F, blood pressure 91/52 mm Hg, and pulse 93/min. He was confused and intermittently agitated, with pupils 3 mm and equal. Cardiovascular exam showed weak peripheral pulses without jugular venous distention or murmurs; lungs were clear; abdomen was soft; no focal neurologic deficits.

Laboratory studies on admission showed features of severe rhabdomyolysis. Serologic testing confirmed chronic hepatitis C but was otherwise unremarkable. Serum toxicology tests were negative for ethanol, acetaminophen, and salicylates. Urine toxicology detected only lorazepam and cotinine but was negative for over 80 other substances, including cannabinoids, cocaine, ecstasy, ephedrine, lysergide, methamphetamine, methylphenidate, oxycodone, and phencyclidine.

Noncontrast CT of the head, MRI of the cervical spine, EEG, and chest and abdominal radiographs were normal. Right upper-quadrant ultrasonography revealed gallbladder calculi, a normal pancreatic duct, and an echogenic right kidney with prominent corticomedullary differentiation.

He received aggressive IV fluids, a norepinephrine infusion, and a bolus of amiodarone. Hyperkalemia was treated with sodium polystyrene sulfonate, calcium gluconate, insulin with glucose, and IV bicarbonate. For severe hyperthermia, he was given dantrolene and placed on cooling blankets. He was sedated, intubated, and mechanically ventilated, and received rasburicase for hyperuricemia. Urine output was 4200 mL over the first 24 hours, then declined to 825 mL and 150 mL over subsequent 24-hour periods. He was started on daily hemodialysis for volume control and solute clearance.

There was no evidence of deep venous thrombosis or soft-tissue infection. He reported a brief gastroenteritis episode at that time. A 39-year-old Caucasian man was referred for evaluation of severe rod–cone retinal dystrophy. He had no history of parental consanguinity. Since childhood he noted high bilateral myopia and nyctalopia; he underwent uneventful bilateral cataract extraction with 13D monofocal intraocular lenses 3 years earlier. His medical history was notable for moderate intellectual disability, transient neutropenia in childhood that resolved spontaneously, microcephaly, truncal obesity, and joint hyperextensibility of the hands, feet, ankles, and knees. He had appropriate social behavior despite intellectual disability. On examination, his facial features included a thick head of hair, bushy eyebrows, a short upturned philtrum, a high nasal bridge with a beak-shaped nose, and an ogival palate.

Fundus examination showed bilateral disc pallor, generalized arteriolar narrowing, mid-peripheral “bone-spicule” pigmentary changes, and retinal pigment epithelium atrophy. Macular optical coherence tomography demonstrated diffuse RPE and outer retinal atrophy involving the subfoveal region without cystoid macular edema. Peripapillary OCT revealed chorioretinal thinning with decreased retinal nerve fiber layer thickness (global RNFL thickness of 53 μm in the right eye and 75 μm in the left eye). Fluorescein angiography showed diffuse RPE atrophy with prominent choroidal vessels and mid-peripheral bone-spicule pigment mobilization. Full-field electroretinography demonstrated absent a- and b-waves in both dark- and light-adapted phases, and pattern ERG lacked a P50 wave. Axial lengths were 26.07 mm (right eye) and 26.13 mm (left eye). 

Thus, the patient presented with a syndromic pigmentary retinal dystrophy characterized electrophysiologically as rod–cone dysfunction with macular involvement, in the setting of high bilateral myopia, presenile cataracts, facial dysmorphism, transient childhood neutropenia, intellectual disability, truncal obesity, joint hyperextensibility, and microcephaly.

On examination, his blood pressure was 88/45 mmHg (responsive to IV fluids), heart rate 96/min, temperature 36.4 °C, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. He weighed 51 kg (BMI 19 kg/m2). A 60-year-old man with a history of heavy cigarette smoking, emphysema, hypertension, and prostate cancer in remission presented with a 4-hour history of acute right lower-quadrant abdominal pain. On admission, he was febrile (38.5°C), hypotensive (systolic blood pressure 90 mmHg), and tachycardic (heart rate 110/min); examination revealed peritonism in the right lower quadrant. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a perforated appendix with a 51×31×26 mm collection and surrounding fat stranding, innumerable hepatic nodules, mural thickening of the cecum and sigmoid colon, and marked mesenteric, para-aortic, and portocaval lymphadenopathy; there was also pulmonary consolidation and collapse in the right lower lobe. The patient underwent exploratory laparotomy, which revealed a perforated appendix with four-quadrant purulent contamination and a thickened, woody sigmoid colon; a subtotal colectomy with end ileostomy was performed. Postoperatively, he remained ventilated. On day 2, CT of the chest for staging demonstrated bulky multi-station mediastinal lymphadenopathy contiguous with soft tissue thickening enveloping the right lower and middle lobe bronchi. An extubation attempt on day 3 failed, and the patient died on day 6 after withdrawal of care.

A 36‐year‐old man of Indian origin presented at 2:30 a.m. with acute right‐sided weakness and three episodes of vomiting. He awoke around midnight with headache and vomiting, then noted right‐sided numbness and weakness; there was no visual change or speech disturbance. He had experienced odd sensations and occasional tremors in his right arm and leg over the prior two weeks but had not sought care. His medical history was unremarkable. He was a nonsmoker, denied alcohol or drug use, and worked as a teacher. 

On examination, pulse was 88 bpm, blood pressure 124/87 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He was alert (GCS 15) with intact speech. Findings included partial left ptosis, bilateral torsional nystagmus on vertical and horizontal gaze, equal reactive pupils, and no ophthalmoplegia. Motor strength was 0/5 in the right upper limb, 3/5 proximally and 2/5 distally in the right lower limb; left‐sided strength was normal. Reflexes were brisk bilaterally with right ankle clonus; the right plantar response was upgoing. Sensation was intact. NIH Stroke Scale score was 7. Cardiorespiratory examination was normal.

Noncontrast CT of the head showed no acute pathology but revealed an incidental 4 × 6 mm hyperdense focus in the left parasagittal frontal cortex suggestive of a cavernoma. CT angiography demonstrated normal opacification of cervical and intracranial arteries; CT perfusion was symmetric. Admission laboratory studies, including complete blood count, coagulation profile, and kidney, liver, and thyroid function tests, were normal except for a total protein of 87 g/L (normal 60–80). Chest radiograph and 12‐lead ECG were normal. Transthoracic echocardiography with bubble study was unremarkable. HbA1c was 5.4%; lipid profile was within normal limits. 

Brain MRI showed a recent ischemic infarction in the left paramedian medulla without hemorrhagic transformation; the small frontal cavernoma was again noted. MR angiography was unremarkable. A diagnosis of ischemic stroke in a 36‐year‐old gentleman with no apparent risk factors was made, and further investigations were initiated to look for the cause.

He reported no back pain, fevers, night sweats, or weight loss and had no history of smoking or known malignancy. On examination, he had full strength throughout all extremities but had decreased sensation from the T3 dermatome downward. He exhibited four beats of clonus bilaterally, hyperreflexia in the lower extremities, and profound ataxia, rendering him unable to walk more than a few steps. 

Contrast-enhanced MRI of the thoracic spine demonstrated a diffusely enhancing lesion centered at T1 with near-circumferential epidural extension causing severe cord compression. CT of the thoracic spine showed an expansile bony lesion of the T1 vertebral body with extension into the left pedicle and posterior elements. CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed no evidence of a primary malignancy, and laboratory studies, including inflammatory markers, were within normal limits. 

Given his rapidly progressive neurological decline, the decision was made to proceed urgently with surgical decompression, spinal stabilization, and tissue diagnosis.

clinical_record:
A 44-year-old woman presented with a two-week history of abnormal behavior, decreased concentration, and postural instability. She had a history of insomnia and irritable bowel syndrome and was taking vitamin D3, vitamin K, manganese, and activated charcoal. She and her parents denied other medications. She had been started on lorazepam by her general practitioner without improvement.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Teeth had a greyish discoloration. Neurologic exam showed confusion, impaired attention, and disorientation. Muscle tone and strength were normal; coordination, sensation, and cranial nerves were intact; there were no pyramidal signs.

While in the emergency department, she became more somnolent and developed frequent myoclonic jerks. Laboratory tests including CBC, renal, hepatic, and thyroid function, CRP, vitamin B12, and folate were normal; syphilis and HIV tests were negative. Noncontrast brain CT was unremarkable. Lumbar puncture showed protein 47 mg/dL (15–45) and 10 WBC/μL (<5). Empiric IV acyclovir and ceftriaxone were started for possible infectious encephalitis.

On the neurology service, she remained moderately drowsy with exuberant generalized myoclonus at rest and on action. EEG revealed generalized background slowing without focal or periodic features. Brain MRI on hospital day 5 was normal. She clinically worsened despite antivirals and antibiotics, so intravenous immunoglobulin was given empirically for presumed autoimmune encephalitis. A trial of levetiracetam 1000 mg/day failed to improve the myoclonus.

She first noted the lesion two years earlier, with gradual enlargement over the past four months. An 8-year-old, previously healthy, fully immunized girl presented with 5 days of intermittent fever followed by abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. She had been at home due to the COVID-19 pandemic; her parents had mild upper respiratory symptoms for 1 week. Outpatient oral antibiotics and IV fluids did not improve her symptoms. She was admitted to surgery with suspected appendicitis; abdominal ultrasonography was normal. Persistent fever, abdominal pain, and the emergence of a rash and conjunctivitis prompted transfer to the pediatric COVID-19 ward. 

On examination, temperature was 38.6 °C. She had bilateral nonpurulent conjunctivitis, erythematous throat, palmar erythema, a strawberry tongue, and an erythema multiforme–type rash; there was no hypotension, lymphadenopathy, or respiratory distress. Cardiac examination revealed a grade II/VI murmur at the left sternal border; lung sounds were normal.

Laboratory tests showed ESR 67 mm/h, CRP 166 mg/L, platelet count 192×10^9/L, hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, and WBC 10.3×10^9/L with 82% neutrophils. Liver and renal function tests were normal. Urinalysis and urine culture were negative. A high-resolution chest CT scan was not indicative of COVID-19. Reverse transcription PCR for SARS-CoV-2 and blood cultures were negative.

clinical_record:
A 25-year-old Hispanic woman of African descent, previously healthy and a non-smoker, presented with a 1-month history of dyspnea on exertion, intermittent dry cough, hyporexia, and unquantified intermittent fever. She delayed care until an acute worsening of dyspnea led to emergency department evaluation, where she developed acute respiratory failure and pulseless electrical activity arrest. After orotracheal intubation and stabilization, she was transferred to our institution.

On arrival, she was sedated on mechanical ventilation. Vital signs were notable for blood pressure 200/140 mmHg, heart rate 100 bpm, respiratory rate 16 bpm, temperature 36 °C, and oxygen saturation 78% on ventilatory support. Physical examination revealed anisocoria (right pupil 5 mm, left 3 mm), jugular venous distension, sinus tachycardia, and bilateral coarse rales; no skin lesions or peripheral edema were present.

Chest radiography showed a homogeneous right paratracheal mediastinal mass compressing and displacing the trachea to the left, with adjacent right upper-lobe infiltrates. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest and neck demonstrated an 11 × 8.6 × 9.5 cm lobulated solid mass arising from the right thoracic operculum/pleura, with a nodular pleural component, mass effect on the right hilum, supra-aortic vessels, and superior vena cava, pneumomediastinum, left pneumothorax, and lytic destruction with cortical fracture of the T1 and T2 vertebrae. Centrilobular opacities in the left upper lobe suggested aspiration pneumonitis.

Laboratory tests showed WBC 13.47 × 10^3/µL (85% neutrophils), hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL, platelets 303 × 10^3/µL, INR 1.39, lactic acid 2.83 mmol/L, C-reactive protein 4.20 mg/dL, LDH 592 U/L, calcium 6.58 mg/dL, phosphorus 3.73 mg/dL; arterial blood gas revealed pH 7.30, PCO2 44.5 mmHg, PO2 122 mmHg, HCO3 22.3 mmol/L, BE –3.7 mmol/L, and SO2 98%. She received dexamethasone and piperacillin/tazobactam. Given the atypical imaging features and concern for possible hematologic malignancy, video-assisted thoracoscopic biopsy was planned to obtain adequate tissue.

clinical_record:
A 67-year-old woman with a 4-day history of fever and cough was admitted to a local hospital, where SARS-CoV-2 infection was confirmed by nasopharyngeal PCR. Five days after admission, her respiratory status worsened, prompting intubation and transfer to the ICU. Her comorbidities included diabetes mellitus with dialysis-dependent nephropathy, angina, prior gastric cancer resection, and spinal‐canal stenosis; she was on an antiplatelet agent.  
On arrival: temperature 34 °C; blood pressure 110/65 mmHg; heart rate 102 beats/min; GCS E1VtM1 under deep sedation. Arterial blood gas (on pressure‐control ventilation: PEEP 8 cmH₂O, PiP 25 cmH₂O, FiO₂ 0.5) showed pH 7.309, PaCO₂ 41.5 mmHg, PaO₂ 78.2 mmHg.  
Laboratory studies: WBC 13,900/µL; CRP 13.1 mg/dL; D-dimer 7.25 µg/mL; APTT 170 s; INR 1.35.  
Chest CT: bilateral ground‐glass opacities with lower-lung predominance. Abdominal CT: no overt abnormalities or thromboembolism, but diffuse edema of the intestine, including the transverse colon, and marked sclerotic changes in abdominal vessels.  
She continued dexamethasone (6 mg/day) and commenced continuous renal replacement therapy. On ICU day 3, cefepime was started for ventilator-associated pneumonia. The APTT fell to 51.5 s, and prophylactic-dose unfractionated heparin was initiated to target an APTT of ~60 s.

A 48-year-old white man, a lifelong non-smoker with a remote bronchoscopic resection of a tracheal carcinoid 17 years earlier, presented with a three-month history of mild hemoptysis and cough without dyspnea. He also noted a non-tender, 2 × 2 cm subcutaneous mass on his left forearm without overlying skin changes. On examination, his vital signs were normal with an oxygen saturation of 94% on room air. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, and coagulation profile, were all within normal limits. A chest CT scan showed a polypoid lesion in the precarinal tracheal region adjacent to the anterior wall. Flexible bronchoscopy revealed a mass arising from the anterior tracheal wall just above the main carina, causing an 80% obstruction of the right main bronchus and 70% obstruction of the left main bronchus. The lesion was resected bronchoscopically with electrocautery, restoring full airway patency without complication. A 27-year-old woman who works as an agricultural laborer was referred with fatigue, malaise, anorexia, and epistaxis. On examination, she was pale, with eczematous plaques on her chest and proximal right arm, and had splenomegaly 6 cm below the costal margin. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7.3 g/dL, white-cell count 4.0×10^9/L, and platelets 23×10^9/L. A peripheral-blood smear revealed lymphoblasts. Flow cytometry was positive for TdT, CD34, CD19, CD10, CD22, and HLA-DR, and bone marrow evaluation confirmed acute lymphoblastic leukemia. The eczematous plaques were treated as contact dermatitis with topical methylprednisolone, resolving rapidly, and induction chemotherapy with hyper-CVAD was initiated. 

On day 8, she developed febrile neutropenia and received piperacillin–tazobactam. Coagulase-negative Staphylococcus species grew in blood cultures, prompting addition of teicoplanin. Persistent fever led to repeat cultures, which grew Enterococcus species, and teicoplanin was replaced with daptomycin. High-resolution chest CT showed nonspecific nodules under 1 cm, and serum galactomannan antigen was negative. After 10 days of fever with an absolute neutrophil count of 20/μL, she reported severe pain in her right arm radiating to her shoulder, suggesting herpes zoster; however, no vesicles were present. On examination, there was a very tender point in the upper lateral scapular region with an underlying vague mass. MRI of the right shoulder demonstrated a focal cystic necrotic lesion between the teres minor and teres major muscles.

A 63-year-old man presented with an 8-month history of painless scrotal swelling. Physical examination revealed bilateral testicular enlargement without tenderness. Scrotal ultrasound showed large, solid masses in both testes. Serum β-human chorionic gonadotropin, α-fetoprotein, and lactate dehydrogenase were all within normal limits. After multidisciplinary discussion, a left radical inguinal orchiectomy was performed. The specimen contained a 7.0 × 6.0 × 4.2 cm tumor confined to the testis with lymphovascular invasion. Histologic examination demonstrated a pleomorphic tumor composed of three distinct cell types: small cells, medium cells, and large cells.

A female infant was born at 35 weeks 4 days’ gestation, weighing 2152 g. She was one of monochorionic diamniotic twins; her identical twin died in utero at 24 weeks. Fetal ultrasound had shown microcephaly and ventricular enlargement. Postnatal MRI of the head revealed microcephaly, marked enlargement of both lateral ventricles without signs of elevated intracranial pressure, and severe thinning of the frontal, parietal, and occipital lobes; the temporal lobes, basal ganglia, thalamus, brain stem, and cerebellum were preserved. No intracranial hematoma or neoplastic lesions were seen. Family history was noncontributory. 

At 1 week of age, examination of the eyes showed very weak light reflexes bilaterally. The anterior chambers were slightly shallow, but there were no pupillary abnormalities, cataracts, strabismus, nystagmus, or ptosis. Funduscopic examination revealed mild optic nerve pallor with suspected peripapillary double-ring sign. The fundus had a faint reddish tone; retinal vessels appeared normal in caliber and reached the periphery. No chorioretinal dysplasia was noted.

clinical_record:
A 23-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of progressive abdominal distension accompanied by early satiety and urinary urgency. She denied pain, weight loss, or systemic symptoms. Her menstrual cycles were normal, and her mother had a history of ovarian cysts. On examination, the abdomen was distended with dull percussion notes but without tenderness or guarding.

Transabdominal ultrasonography revealed a cyst measuring 16 × 24 cm that compressed adjacent abdominal organs. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography showed a large midline intraperitoneal cyst, 30 × 25.6 × 16.8 cm in size, extending from the liver to the pelvis and involving the uterus and ovaries. The lesion had a fluid density of 20 Hounsfield units and demonstrated no calcifications, soft-tissue components, or enhancing septations, suggesting a benign etiology.

Laboratory studies, including α-fetoprotein, carcinoembryonic antigen, cancer antigen 19-9, and cancer antigen 125, were all within normal limits; the Risk of Malignancy Algorithm (ROMA) score was 4.1 %. Serological testing for Echinococcus granulosus was negative. A giant intra-abdominal cyst was diagnosed preoperatively, and laparoscopic cyst aspiration with exploration under general anesthesia was planned.
